name: Design Sprint
use_case: A leadership group has been going round in circles for months about whether to back a big new idea, such as a new digital service or a new way of informing parents, and the money is about to be released on the strength of opinions alone. It wants to settle the question in one intensive, time-boxed week: the people who matter, including whoever has the final say, work on it together without interruption, turn the idea into a realistic-looking mock-up, and watch a handful of real future customers or residents try it before anything is funded or built.
strengths: replaces months of meetings and opinion with one week that ends in observed reactions
the person with the final say takes part, so the outcome turns into a decision rather than another round of discussion
a fake but convincing mock-up is cheap to build and cheap to throw away
structured individual sketching and silent voting keep loud voices and seniority from settling the question
a clear result either way: an idea that fails on Friday has cost five days, not a budget year
weaknesses: needs a decision-maker and a cross-functional team of up to about seven people free for five consecutive days
five one-to-one tests reveal whether people understand and can use the idea, not whether enough of them will want or adopt it
overkill for small or well-understood questions, and too short for problems nobody has researched at all
can turn into innovation theatre: an energising week whose results are never acted on
in public bodies, procurement, data-protection and legal rules may limit what can be shown to residents and who may build it
use_cases: The management board of a public agency must decide next month whether to fund a major new service it has debated at length; instead of another round of position papers, it wants its key staff to spend five consecutive days building a believable mock-up and observing five citizens using it.

An education authority is split over a proposed new format for informing families about starting school, and wants the people who will decide to spend one concentrated week shaping a single version and showing it to a few parents before the budget meeting.

A young company is about to invest its seed money in a new offering that exists only as slides and conviction; the founders want to see, before writing any code, whether a handful of target customers understand a convincing facade of it and can actually use it.

A ministry policy team wants to know whether a new idea for guiding young people through their options makes sense to them, and would rather find out in a week with a rough version than after a full programme has been commissioned.
